Mangroves are critical to the Indian River Lagoon ecosystem because they not only help to stabilize the shorelines, but they also serve as a nursery and safe haven for juvenile fish along with many other species native to the lagoon. The project was started in 1995 through the Environmental Learning Center (ELC), until 2008 when it was transferred to the Florida Department of Environmental ProtectionÌs Office of Coastal and Aquatic Managed Areas (FDEP CAMA) Indian River Lagoon Aquatic Preserves Field Office. The project boundary extends from SR 528 in Brevard County to Jupiter Inlet in Palm Beach County.

Lemon Bay is designated as the Lemon Bay Aquatic Preserve and is managed to protect and restore submerged habitats, including seagrass, fish and shellfish. Bay scallop populations declined in the 1960s, primarily due to over harvest. Recovery of bay scallop populations requires adequate sources of larvae, especially following red tide events. Over 2 million bay scallop larvae, collected from nearshore waters in the Florida Panhandle, were released into Lemon Bay over healthy seagrass beds just prior to the stage in their life cycle where they settle onto the seagrass and develop into juvenile scallops. The purpose of the larval release was to provide adequate numbers of juvenile scallops to grow to adulthood and spawn the following fall in Lemon Bay. Monitoring of adult populations and next yearÌs recruitment of larvae is planned. The project involved local, state and regional agencies, as well as volunteers.

Several attempts have been made to stabilize the shoreline of MC-2 by planting marsh grasses and mangroves on the island. Due to the intense wave energy in the area, the success of these restoration efforts has been limited. In an effort to implement a long-term solution to the MC-2 erosion problem, Martin County built a wave attenuation system to stabilize and protect the shoreline of MC-2. The wave attenuation system is essentially an off-shore breakwater comprised of limestone rock. The length of the system is 450 feet. The County chose this particular design because it provides the most effective means of reducing wave energy and has the fewest negative impacts of the available options.

Project_Name: Seeding of Eyed Oyster Larvae onto Recycled Shell Reefs -- Ft. Pierce IRL
Project_Description: Tremendous losses of oyster reefs had occurred in the St. Lucie River Estuary due to physical changes to the watershed, pollution, erosion and hurricanes. The main objective of this project was to create four oyster reefs near the Evans-Crary Bridge in the St. Lucie Estuary (SLE) in Stuart, FL (see RCDB #2487) and two control oyster reefs in Indian River Lagoon (IRL) in Ft. Pierce, FL.  Two of the reefs in the SLE and one reef in the IRL were seeded with oyster larvae inside containment booms to jumpstart their propagation.  The seeding of these reefs helped to create a more stable seed source.  Along with restoring oyster reefs and their associated species, the project enabled us to determine if this restoration approach would work in an area where oysters and their substrate have been completely obliterated with little or no available seed source. Benefits of the project beyond the restored oyster reef include improved water quality, increased public awareness of oyster reefs and their value to aquatic ecosystems, shoreline stabilization and improvement in fisheries habitat.

Project_Name: Seeding of Eyed Oyster Larvae onto Recycled Shell Reefs -- St. Lucie Estuary

The seeding of these reefs helps to create a more stable seed source.  Along with restoring oyster reefs and their associated species, the project enabled us to determine if this restoration approach would work in an area where oysters and their substrate have been completely obliterated with little or no available seed source.

Project_Name: Indian River Lagoon Restoration- St. Lucie and Loxahatchee Rivers Oyster Project
Project_Description: This project restored 26 acres of oyster reef habitat within the St. Lucie Estuary and the Loxahatchee River systems. More than 30 million pounds of limestone and oyster shell cultch were deployed to construct a series of small patch oyster reefs.  Oyster reefs provide much needed substrate for oyster spat recruitment. In addition, these restoration efforts will help improve water quality in both rivers enabling expanded growth of seagrass and supporting both estuarine and marine fish nurseries. These reefs provide habitat structure for other species, including shrimp, clams, crabs, snails and a variety of fish, including many economically important species such as gag grouper, gray snapper, sheepshead, and red drum.  Enhancing oyster populations in this area also contributed to the goals of the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan

Project_Name: St. Lucie Estuary Oyster Reef Habitat Restoration Project
Project_Description:
The purpose of the St. Lucie Estuary (SLE) Oyster Reef Habitat Restoration Project is to restore historic oyster reef habitat and improve shoreline stability. By restoring approximately 2 acres of oyster reef habitat, and creating stretches of living shoreline, in the SLE, the project furthers the Estuary Restoration Act's mission to protect and restore marine and coastal habitats.  The project also furthers NOAAÌs coastal resiliency objectives due to the fact that oyster reef restoration combined with living shorelines can help to protect against stresses caused by sea level rise/climate change.  

By leveraging the ERA funds with St. Lucie River Issues Team grant funds, the County was able to increase the constructed oyster reef acreage to 4.52 acres during the summer of 2013. The living shoreline component of oyster shell bags, oyster domes and saltmarsh planting was completed early summer 2014.  959 volunteers contributed 2133 hours to the living shoreline component of the project.  This project will post-restoration monitoring efforts through the fall of 2017.

Project_Name: Threatened Coral Recovery and Restoration Phase IV_Florida
Project_Description: The Nature Conservancy (TNC) and project partners built upon Acropora coral recovery and restoration work that was piloted with TNC-NOAA Community-based Habitat Restoration Grant Program (CRP) support beginning in 2004.  This project was scaled up dramatically with American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA) funding provided by NOAAÌs Restoration Center in 2009.  The project capitalized on these previous efforts by maintaining a minimum of 10,000 corals in established nurseries managed by TNC and its partners, and outplanting 8,000 additional corals to degraded reefs over two years.  By building on work previously supported by NOAA, this project will contribute significantly to the recovery of federally listed staghorn coral (Acropora cervicornis) and elkhorn coral (Acropora palmata) and restoration of some of AmericaÌs most significant coral reefs.  Additionally, acroporid corals provide structural complexity that is important to many commercially and recreationally important fish species (Bruckner, 2002) so by restoring them the project will also help enhance the fisheries and tourism-based economies that they support.  The project was implemented in 8 subregions of the Florida and USVI reef systems, with nursery and restoration sites located in each subregion.  See map for St. Thomas and St. Croix records.

Project_Name: Upper Florida Keys Coral Population Enhancement through Active Propagation - CRF
Project_Description: This project addresses restoration actions to help recover Acropora cervicornis (staghorn coral) and A. palmata (elkhorn coral), two coral species that are listed as ÏThreatenedÓ under the Endangered Species Act.   Staghorn (9,925) and elkhorn (4,100) corals will be transplanted from Coral Reef Foundation nurseries to reefs at densities and sizes that exceed what is found within the natural population.  Relatively large corals (>25cm to 45cm diameter) will be grown in nurseries and transplanted to various reef sites in the Florida Keys.  Through careful hypothesis-driven monitoring, whether or not clusters and thickets that approximate pre-dieoff densities will be more resilient to existing disturbances will be tested. The project will also address developing offshore nursery techniques for three additional species of stony coral that have been nominated for listing as endangered under the US Endangered Species Act (Montastrea faveolata, Montastrea annularis, and Dendrogyra cylindricus).

Project_Name: Florida Keys Shallow Sponge Restoration Phase I

Project_Name: Florida Keys Shallow Sponge Restoration Phase II
Project_Description: We have expanded a past NOAA-TNC Community Restoration Project to increase our restoration footprint and better assess the restoration of hard-bottom sponge communities. We have: (a) added more restoration sites, (b) broadened the taxonomic diversity of sponges on restoration sites, and (c) expanded our monitoring beyond measures of sponge transplant success to include assessment of the restoration of ecological function, especially as essential nursery habitat for fish and invertebrates. We also will explore the potential for the restoration of reef-dwelling sponges in a preliminary study in collaboration with NOAA supported scientists working on coral restoration along the Florida Keys reef tract.

67-acres of borrow pits within the Loxahatchee watershed has been restored to natural wetland grades and planted with native vegetation. The 250-acre Jupiter Ranch tract is a portion of the cypress Creek basin in Palm Beach County, north of Indiantown Road and east of Gulfstream Road that was partially cleared and drained, primarily for agriculture purposes, most recently for cattle ranching. The western portion of Cypress Creek in Palm Beach County was most recently restored with funding assistance from the Loxahatchee River Preservation Initiative. The Jupiter Ranch Restoration Project, includes the removal of exotic vegetation from the project area, the restoration and creation of wetlands from areas that have been mined for shell rock, and replanting areas that have been cleared. The project began in spring 2010 with mechanical treatment of exotic vegetation. The mechanical treatment primarily focused on Australian pine from the spoil piles that were left behind from the shell mining and was followed by ground control treatment of exotic vegetation, primarily Brazilian pepper, Melaleuca, Australian pine, and Old World climbing fern in the project area. License Plate funding was used for the final phase of this project, restoring and/or creating approximately 67-acres of wetlands from the shell borrow pit areas. The areas were contoured to more natural wetland grades and elevations, then native vegetation was planted along trails, wetlands and buffer lands. A majority of the 67-acres of wetlands re-vegetated naturally.

Project_Name: Cedar Key - Marine Debris into Oyster Reefs
Project_Description:
The proposed project includes the reclamation and restoration of the following three primary areas: 
1)  reclamation of  about 1.0 acres of state-owned submerged lands included in a minimum of 28 two-acre shellfish aquaculture leases in the Gulf of Mexico (number of leases of participating leaseholders), or partial reclamation of 56 acres of leases; 
2)  construction of a 0.15-acre oyster reef that will protect about 400 linear feet of shoreline and a 0.4-acre seagrass recovery site adjacent to Atsena Otie Key; and 
3)  enhancement of about 100 feet of oyster reef habitat (0.02 acres) at Corrigans Reef in Waccasassa Bay.

Since the 1980Ìs, oyster reef habitat has declined precipitously in FloridaÌs Big Bend region of the Gulf of Mexico.
To mitigate these declines, this oyster restoration project incorporates two new techniques in oyster restoration: (1) use of bagged building blocks of living oysters transplanted to create instant living reefs that are resilient to wave action, and (2) designing reefs to capture and protect extant oyster spat and increase growth and survival by enhancing water flow around reef structure in a way that allows built reefs to naturally expand.

One thousand twenty linear feet of Charles Ringling era (1920Ìs) seawall were in extremely poor condition on the eastern shoreline of Sarasota Bay. Located on the New College of Florida campus, the area is designated as a Caples-Ringling Estates National Historic District on the National Register of Historic Places. The failing gravity seawall was removed and a 1500 square foot dock was demolished. To maintain the integrity of the historic district, a new seawall was constructed along the southern 500Ì of shoreline. The new seawall is topped by a historically correct balustrade and a wide esplanade. Along the northern 520 feet of the shoreline, a new intertidal lagoon was created landward of the historic seawall. The deepest part of the lagoon is -2 feet (NAVD 88). The lagoon has sloping intertidal shorelines planted in native bayfront vegetation. Several remnant sections of the historic wall serve as a temporary breakwater to protect the new lagoon.

Project_Description: Siesta Waterway Pilot Mulching and Planting project is one component of a larger goal to reduce erosion, provide greater habitat diversity and improve the natural aesthetics of the waterway. While the project restores only a small area of habitat, it provides large community stewardship and education opportunities, water quality improvements, research data on the effectiveness of restoration methods and partnership between the Civic Association and County for future components of naturalizing the waterway.

Coastal wetlands are among the most biologically productive natural ecosystems on Earth. Unfortunately, on FloridaÌs northeast and east-central coasts, wetlands were historically considered mosquito factories, uninviting wastelands with no inherent value. For decades, the Indian River LagoonÌs wetlands were filled, ditched and diked Û mostly to control mosquito populations, with little regard for the other ecological values they provided. By the 1970s, more than 40,000 acres of coastal wetlands (approximately 75 percent of the lagoonwide total) were impounded and isolated from the lagoon. Pumping water into these isolated impoundments stopped most mosquito production, but also impacted the vegetation and many wetland functions. This project is phase 2 of wetland restoration, management, and water quality improvement to an impounded swamp adjacent to the Indian River Lagoon in St. Lucie County. Prior to impoundment, the swamp was a healthy mangrove marsh. During this phase the quad pump station was completed in the dike. The pump station helps to continue restoring this impoundment area to a more natural hydrology, allowing exchange of water to the lagoon. The quality, clarity, and circulation of waters of an additional 26-acre restored wetland and of the waters of the Lagoon immediately off shore from the project area are significantly improved by the restored filtering function of the mangrove marsh and seasonal pumping of waters into the wetland. Additional phases will add educational nature trails, and information kiosks to the site.

Project_Name: Restoration of dragline ditched coastal wetlands in Volusia County, Florida: Phase 1
Project_Description: Dragline ditches are extensive networks of deep, wide ditches and spoil piles cut through historical coastal wetland habitat, severely reducing the acreage of wetlands remaining. The purpose of the ditches was to interrupt the life cycle of saltmarsh mosquitoes by altering their breeding sites. A systematic process for restoring coastal wetlands that have been dragline ditched has been developed. Dragline ditch restoration projects such as this one require the use of an amphibious excavator. An excavator was mounted on tracked pontoons, enabling them to access submerged areas. This low-bearing weight machine (less than 2 pounds per square inch) is owned and operated by Volusia County Mosquito Control. Vegetation was cleared from the spoil area and placed in the adjacent ditch. This process avoided burning the plants and permanently sequesters the carbon they contain. Spoil material was first moved to the side of the ditch. If additional material remained, the main ditch was narrowed. The area of the spoil pile and the newly filled ditch were carefully graded to the adjacent remaining wetland elevation. The result is that substantially more area is at coastal wetland elevation.

Project_Name: Habitat Creation for Subadult Fish Populations in Tampa Bay
Project_Description: Installation of Ledge Mimic Modules and reef balls provide habitat for hundreds of subadult grouper, snapper, and grunt, replacing habitat lost to dredging and providing protection from predators for the subadult life stage.

The primary project goal is removal of the upland mounds throughout the site to restore historic hydrology. The mounds are being removed using the hydroblasting technique. Exotic vegetation on the mounds is removed and the mound material is spread in 360-degree direction using high pressure water jet. Each mound is reduced to an elevation below mean high water to eliminate the uplands and improve tidal flow. Once the mounds are reduced below mean high tides, they will be planted with smooth cord grass. Phase II of the project is currently being permitted as additional funding is already secured

Restoration included removing exotic species and planting the area with a greater diversity of native riparian species.

Project_Name: Cockroach Bay Seagrass Management Through Restoration and Assessment
Project_Description: In partnership with NOAA's CRP and the SARP, the Environmental Protection Commission of Hillsborough County restored seagrass beds within the Cockroach Bay Aquatic Preserve through the creation of pole and troll zones (no motor) and also by transplanting seagrass.  The project transplanted seagrass both inside and outside of the pole and troll zones to compare techniques. Data collected during the implementation of this study found that the prop scars in Halodule were recovering at a very fast rate- faster than it took to implement restoration. It was decided to utilize monies forfeited buy another project and incorporate a seagrass transplanting project in Tampa bay, but not in Cockroach Bay. Hillsborough EPC partnered with Tampa Bay Watch to restore 0.27 acres of seagrass near the MacDill air Force Base. Planting was completed in Early Sept. 2012.

The purpose of this project was to restore seagrass in areas of Hillsborough Bay where they have existed historically.  The project, also, encouraged greater stewardship of Tampa BayÌs natural resources by providing hands-on educational experiences for community and student volunteers. Manatee grass was transplanted from a permitted donor site by staff, students and 53 community volunteers, who dedicated over 300 hours to the project. After one year, the project demonstrated that not only had the 1,200 m? transplanted manatee grass been restored to the area, but that it expanded beyond the initial planting site, resulting in approximately 2,800m? of restored seagrass beds.  Many fish and shellfish species will benefit from the restored habitat and water quality improvements are expected on continue due to the expansion of the seagrass beds.  The project is part of an interagency effort to evaluate seagrass transplanting and restoration techniques and supports the larger Longshore Bar Restoration Project ongoing in Hillsborough Bay.

More than 3,000 salt marsh plants were planted by student and teacher volunteers. Salt marsh (Spartina alterniflora) is utilized for shoreline stabilization and habitat enhancement at the project location. Salt marsh has numerous benefits for Tampa Bay and its marine and shoreline inhabitants: stabilizes shorelines and protects against erosion, provides habitat for small fish and other creatures, traps sediments that would otherwise sweep into the bay. Salt marsh communities are critically important habitats that grow along the intertidal fringe of the bay, preventing erosion, absorbing pollutants, and providing habitat for important fish and wildlife species.

Project_Name: MacDill Airforce Base Salt Marsh and Oyster Restoration - Phase II
Project_Description: NOAA Fisheries partnered with MacDill Air Force Base and Tampa Bay Watch to restore nearly one acre of oyster habitat and salt marsh in northeast Tampa Bay. The restoration site is located along a point of land at the Air Force base that is experiencing high rates of erosion due to wave energy. 25 volunteers contributed 100 hours planting salt marsh grass plugs along the shoreline immediately behind the created oyster reef. Funding for this project was provided through a partnership between NOAA's Community-based Restoration Program and Restore America's Estuaries.

This restoration project helped to stabilize the shoreline and restore fisheries habitat at the Richard T. Paul Alafia Bank Bird Sanctuary in eastern Hillsborough Bay in Tampa, Florida. This island has been eroding over the years due to large boat wakes caused by ship traffic in this stretch of Tampa Bay.  This project installed a series of pyramid shaped wave attenuation devices along 250 ft. of shoreline to reduce erosion and stabilize the habitat behind this installed reef.  This project helped to leverage more than 650 ft. of additional shoreline restoration along the Bird Sanctuary.  In addition, the area behind the wave attenuation devices was planted with saltmarsh species to help jumpstart natural recruitment.

Prescribed fire was used to control invasive species, improve wildlife habitat, reduce hazardous fuel loads, and promote new growth for foraging. A separate area was targeted for invasives control using herbicide application. This area had several spots of established invasives that had persisted despite previous applications.

Work in 2013 included the chemical treatment of Brazilian pepper and other non-native, invasive species across two quadrants of the base (1,011 acres). Invasive trees and grasses were treated through a mixture of foliar application and girdling to kill the plants in place. Following the initial herbicide applications, contractors were responsible to retreat invasive plant species within the project area until the plants were completely dead. No further removal or treatment was required after the invasive species were killed, and plants were left to breakdown over time. The project area included 1,011) acres of upland forest and open fields (known as Quadrant 1, and Quadrant 2B). In addition, the mechanical clearing of live and dead Brazilian pepper was accomplished on a 10 acre site in Quadrant 3B.

This project has enhanced/restored 111.45 ac of various estuarine, freshwater, and coastal upland habitats. Portions of base and golf course stormwater runoff were re-routed through wetlands that will provide some cleansing of potential pollutants prior to draining to Tampa Bay. Excavation/creation of the new wetlands typically was adjacent and complementary to existing wetlands and/or upland communities. Primary land clearing (i.e., non-native vegetation), excavation, and contouring were accomplished using trackhoes and bulldozers. Plant and trash debris and soils/sediments were loaded and hauled away via trackhoes, front-end loaders, and dump trucks

Project_Name: CORE Program- McKay Bay and Schultz Nature Preserve Restoration
Project_Description: Tampa Bay Watch implemented two community-based oyster restoration projects as part of the Community Oyster Reef Enhancement (CORE) Program.  This program, led by Tampa Bay Watch, is a partnership between government agencies, schools and other community-based groups designed to restore impacted estuary shorelines and promote environmental awareness in the community.  Benefits of oyster habitat restoration include the improvement of water quality through natural biological filtration and the creation of habitat for other marine organisms.  In 2012 and 2013, funded sites included McKay Bay, which is managed by the Tampa Port Authority, and the Schultz Nature Preserve, which is managed by Hillsborough County Parks Department.  During this project, Tampa Bay Watch hosted more than 25 events.  These events garnered the support of 236 volunteers that contributed more than 700 hours to create oyster reef habitat.

Project_Name: Community Marsh Habitat Restoration- Rock Ponds and Bahia Beach
Project_Description: This project conducted saltmarsh plantings at the Rock Ponds Ecosystem site and the Bahia Beach Habitat Restoration site.  The project supported Tampa Bay Watch's 17 school-based wetland plant nurseries and restored 13.2 acres of saltmarsh habitat.  To accomplish this project, Tampa Bay Watch hosted more than 20 planting events utilizing more than 4,000 volunteers.

Project_Name: San Carlos Bay-Bunche Beach Preserve Restoration
Project_Description: This project includes habitat restoration at the existing 704 acre San Carlos Bay Bunche Beach Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan has been developed for the Preserve which focuses on restoration of upland, wetland and beach habitats, as well as public access, education and stewardship. Environmental educational activities are provided to the Lee County Public Schools, Edison College, FL Gulf Coast University and the public. FY12 Restoration activities completed by staff, volunteers and FL Gulf Coast University students include removal of over 500 pounds of invasive exotic vegetation and trash, as well as volunteer guided nature walks.

Project_Name: Clam Bayou Mangrove, SAV, and Oyster Restoration Project
Project_Description: Clam Bayou is a shallow, mangrove-lined lagoon located on Sanibel Island, FL, and is adjacent to one of the most visited natural mangrove areas in the country, providing highly visible efforts and outreach opportunities. Degradation of Clam Bayou habitats served as the impetus for the mangrove, seagrass, and shellfish restoration activities which restored nearly 1.5 acres of estuarine fisheries habitat. These efforts included planting of red mangrove propagules and seagrasses, oyster reef construction using bagged oyster shell, and monitoring.

Project_Name: Clam Bayou Oyster Reef Restoration and Evaluation of Seagrass and Water Quality
Project_Description: The project will construct approximately 0.2 acres of intertidal oyster reefs near a newly constructed flow-way in Clam Bayou in Sanibel, FL.  The reef will be made from bagged fossilized oyster shell.  Monitoring will be conducted for the created oyster reefs as well as on the impact to adjacent seagrass beds.

Project_Name: Gasparilla Sound/Charlotte Harbor Aquatic Preserve Phase 2 Scallop Restoration
Project_Description: Approximately 10 million bay scallop larvae, collected from nearshore waters in the Florida Big Bend area, were released over healthy seagrass beds just prior to the stage in their life cycle where they settle onto the seagrass and develop into juvenile scallops. An additional 18,000 juvenile bay scallops were raised to 5-20mm size and released, also in seagrass beds. Monitoring of adult populations and next yearÌs recruitment of larvae is planned. The project involved local, state and regional agencies, as well as volunteers.

Project_Name: Pine Island Sound Scallop Restoration Cage Program Phase 3
Project_Description: To improve the scallop population, cages with juvenile scallops (scallop "seed") were deployed in seagrass beds. Scallops grew to reproductive size inside the cases and spawned into surrounding seagrass beds in Tarpon Bay. SCCF staff and volunteers maintain the cages and collect monthly scallop data including survival, size and reproductive state, which helps scientists understand how local scallops live, grow and reproduce.

Project_Name: The Dunes Floating Vegetated Wetlands in Stormwater Ponds
Project_Description: Artificial floating wetlands (500 square feet) were installed in the stormwater ponds in The Dunes residential golf community to reduce nutrients and improve water quality in the pond and discharges.

This is an extensive habitat restoration project at the 37,199  acre Myakka River State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. There is an approved management plan for the park and management focuses on habitat and hydrologic restoration and public access. Restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and removal of non-native vegetation and animals, to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed included 10,688 acres of prescribed fire, as well as exotic plant and animal removal and trail maintenance.

This project includes habitat and hydrologic restoration at the 268 acre Smokehouse Bay Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan has been developed for the Preserve which focuses on habitat and hydrologic restoration, including invasive exotic vegetation and animal removal and back filling ditches. FY12 restoration activities completed by staff and contractors included restoring the natural elevation on the abandoned agriculture fields, backfilling the old mosquito control ditches, removing Brazilian pepper and Australian pines, and removing 90 feral hogs.

This project includes habitat restoration at the existing 730 acre Pine Island Flatwoods Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan has been developed for the Preserve which focuses on habitat restoration and public stewardship and access. During FY12, contractors, staff and volunteers from Lee County Conservation 2020 and Calusa Land trust completed roller chopping of 15 acres of palmettos, logging of Melaleuca, removing other invasive exotic plants, planting long leaf and slash pines and trail maintenance.

Project_Name: Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park Cape Coral Restoration
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 7,951 acre Cape Coral Management Area of the Charlotte Harbor Preserve State Park managed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. There is an approved management plan for the area and management focuses on habitat restoration and public access. Restoration activities focus on prescribed fire and removal of non-native vegetation and animals, to improve wildlife habitat. FY12 restoration activities completed included 143 acres of prescribed fire, as well as road and trail maintenance.

This is a habitat restoration project at the 59 acre Matanzas Pass Preserve managed by Lee County 2020. A management plan has been developed for the Preserve which focuses on invasive exotic plant removal, native vegetation planting, debris removal and public educational and recreational activities, including boardwalks, trails and canoe/kayak launch. A native plant and animal species list has been developed for the preserve. FY12 restoration activities conducted by staff and volunteers included removal of air potato, Brazilian pepper and Australian pine, planting native wildflowers and trail maintenance.

This is a habitat and hydrologic restoration project at the 2,654 acre Prairie Pines Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan has been developed for the Preserve which focuses on habitat and hydrologic restoration, as well as public access, including hiking and horseback riding. Activities include restoration of hydrology from off-road vehicle trails and removal of invasive exotic plants and exotic animals. FY12 restoration activities completed by Lee County staff and volunteers included removal of 150 feral hogs and Melaleuca and treatment of Guinea grass, old world climbing fern and cogongrass, as well as trail and sign maintenance.

The Briarcliff Filter Marsh Project is managed by Lee County and is implemented to improve water quality. The project is located along Briarcliff Canal which leads to Ten Mile Canal before entering Mullock Creek, a tributary to Estero Bay Aquatic Preserve. The project consists of a constructed 15 acre filter marsh designed to provide wetlands that will filter water from the surrounding residential and industrial land uses and impervious areas. Water will enter the filter marsh by two control structures and a steel sheet-pile weir was installed to aid in the dry season water conservation.

This project includes habitat restoration at the 4.3 acre Mullock Creek Preserve managed by Lee County Conservation 2020. A management plan for the Preserve has been developed which focuses on habitat and hydrologic restoration on the native and disturbed wetlands and uplands. However, public access is not planned due to the small size and location, limiting access points. FY12 restoration activities include treating of invasive exotic vegetation, including Melaleuca, Brazilian pepper, Java plum, earleaf acacia.
